title: Boys & Men Falling Behind
scope: Male disadvantage in education, work and well-being.
primary_image_prompt:
A minimalist flat vector-style icon illustration, in a clean editorial line-art style: one compact scene grouped in the center with wide white margins, nothing touching the edges: a large pair of men's leather work boots standing side by side on the crest of a small rounded hill as the dominant focal mass, outlined and filled; a small pair of boy's sneakers standing just in front of them, overlapping the toe of the nearer boot; a winding footpath crossing the whole hill from left to right, passing the boots; at its left end a small one-room schoolhouse with a bell, at its right end a small workshop building with a wide roll-up door; one plain round sun low behind the hill.

Composition: one dominant focal mass with smaller supporting elements at clearly different scales (big, medium, small); at least one element overlaps another so the scene has depth; the ground is a gentle curve, never a flat line; one connective element runs across the frame to tie the pieces together. A single coherent scene, not a row of separate objects. Centered with generous, even padding.

Style: monoline line art with ONE uniform stroke weight on every element, including the thinnest wisps and lines. Rounded line caps and corners. Confident, slightly bold strokes so it stays legible when small. No fussy internal detail.

Color: a single hue, two tones only. Draw all lines in solid #9459a2, and give every major mass a clearly visible soft fill of the same hue at about 15-18% opacity, so the duotone is obviously present rather than white interiors. No other colors, no gradients, no shadows, no 3D, no texture.

Important: NO border, NO frame, NO box or outline around the scene, just the illustration on a plain white background. No text, letters, or numbers. No human figures or faces. Calm, neutral, editorial mood: show the subject plainly, neither celebrating nor warning. Also avoid: no people, no faces, no hands, no silhouettes of men or boys, no gender symbols, no race track or finish line, no ladder, no arrows, no trophy, no podium, no broken or tattered objects, no tears, no flags, no text or numbers.

overview.summary: Girls now outpace boys in school and college, and men die younger. The central argument is whether the cause is sex or disadvantage.
overview.scope_covered: Gaps between the sexes in school, college, work, health and friendship, what causes them, and the remedies on offer.
overview.scope_excluded: Loneliness in general, AI and jobs, and the cost of college, which have their own pages; gender identity and women’s rights debates such as abortion, except where they enter the comparison.
overview.why_now: On November 18, 2026 the American Institute for Boys and Men held its first national summit in Washington, where California Governor Gavin Newsom said more than 11,000 men had joined a state service challenge set up under his 2025 order on boys and men.
overview.why_now_source_label: Office of the Governor of California

stats.label: Women’s share of US bachelor’s degrees
stats.note: Women earned 58.5 percent of US bachelor’s degrees in 2021–22, up from 43.1 percent in 1969–70; they first passed half in 1981–82.
stats.detail: In 2021–22 US colleges awarded 1,179,719 bachelor’s degrees to women and 835,316 to men, so women earned about 344,000 more; in 1969–70 men had earned about 110,000 more than women. Women’s lead was wider at other levels that year: 62.8 percent of associate’s degrees, 62.6 percent of master’s degrees and 57.0 percent of doctor’s degrees. The table projects a 59.3 percent share of bachelor’s degrees for 2022–23. Those who see a crisis for boys treat the reversal as its clearest single sign; those who doubt the crisis framing note that men still dominate the highest-paying majors, such as engineering and computer science, and that the gap is widest among Black and low-income students.
stats.source_label: National Center for Education Statistics, Digest of Education Statistics 2023, Table 318.10

stats.label: Men’s share of US suicide deaths
stats.note: Men were about 80 percent of the 48,824 Americans who died by suicide in 2024, at an age-adjusted rate of 22.3 per 100,000 against women’s 5.6.
stats.detail: That was 38,977 men and 9,847 women, and a male rate about four times the female rate. Both rates fell slightly from 2023, when they were 22.7 for men and 5.9 for women. Among men the rate rises with age, from 20.2 per 100,000 at ages 15 to 24 to 29.6 at 45 to 64 and 40.1 at 75 and over. Firearms were the leading means for both sexes. The male excess sits beside what researchers call the gender paradox in suicide: girls and women report suicidal thoughts and attempts more often than males do.
stats.source_label: NCHS Data Brief No. 572, “Changes in Suicide Rates in the United States From 2023 to 2024”

stats.label: Prime-age men in the US labor force
stats.note: In 2025, 89.4 percent of American men aged 25 to 54 were working or looking for work, down from 97.3 percent in 1954.
stats.detail: The roughly 11 percent outside the labor force are neither working nor looking. The decline ran slowly from the 1960s to the mid-2010s, reaching 88.2 percent in 2014 and 87.9 percent in the pandemic year 2020, and has recovered modestly since. Over the same period the rate for women aged 25 to 54 rose from 38.7 percent in 1954 to 77.8 percent in 2025 (BLS series LNU01300062), so the gap between the sexes has narrowed from both directions. Among men without a degree who are out of work, about half cite illness or disability, according to the American Institute for Boys and Men (2024).
stats.source_label: US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Current Population Survey, series LNU01300061

stats.label: Women’s earnings as a share of men’s, US
stats.note: Women working full time had median weekly earnings 83 percent of men’s in 2024, up from 62 percent in 1979; the ratio was 88 to 91 percent among workers under 35.
stats.detail: The figure compares all women and all men who work full time, not men and women in the same job with the same hours and experience. It has stayed between 81 and 84 percent since 2010, and it is 77 to 81 percent among workers aged 35 and over. Economists, notably the Nobel laureate Claudia Goldin, attribute much of the widening after the mid-thirties to the arrival of children, which cuts mothers’ hours and pay more than fathers’. At the top, a record 55 women led Fortune 500 companies in 2026, 11 percent of the list (Fortune, 2026). Those who doubt that men as a group are falling behind cite these figures; those who see a male crisis reply that averages and top jobs describe an elite and hide the decline of men at the bottom.
stats.source_label: US Bureau of Labor Statistics, “Highlights of women’s earnings in 2024” (Report 1117)

stats.label: US high school students reporting distress, by sex
stats.note: In 2023, 52.6 percent of US high school girls reported persistent sadness or hopelessness, against 27.7 percent of boys; girls were also about twice as likely to have considered or attempted suicide.
stats.detail: For seriously considering suicide the shares were 27.1 percent of girls and 14.1 percent of boys. The survey asks students about their own feelings and behavior over the past year, so it measures reported distress, not deaths. Girls fare worse than boys on almost every measure of self-reported mental health in it, which makes it the evidence most often cited against the view that boys are worse off in every respect. Whether reported distress or deaths, which run the other way, is the better gauge of who is suffering more is itself disputed.
stats.source_label: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Youth Risk Behavior Survey 2023, MMWR Supplement 73(4)

stats.label: Boys’ share of out-of-school suspensions, US
stats.note: Boys were 70.5 percent of the 2,510,919 US public school students suspended out of school in 2017–18, and 72.8 percent of the 101,958 expelled.
stats.detail: Boys are about half of public school students, so they were suspended at more than twice the rate of girls. The same table shows large racial gaps as well: Black students accounted for 925,864 of the suspensions, more than White students’ 795,834, although Black students are a much smaller share of enrollment. Whether the sex gap reflects boys’ behavior, the way schools respond to it, or both is one of the central disputes over whether schools shortchange boys. Federal data for later years exist, but 2017–18 is the last full pre-pandemic year in this table.
stats.source_label: National Center for Education Statistics, Digest of Education Statistics 2022, Table 233.30

stats.label: Life expectancy at birth in the US, by sex
stats.note: An American boy born in 2024 could expect to live 76.5 years and a girl 81.4, a gap of 4.9 years, down from 5.3 in 2023.
stats.detail: Life expectancy for the whole population rose to 79.0 years in 2024, up 0.6 year; men’s rose from 75.8 and women’s from 81.1. The gap narrowed in a year when overdose deaths, which fall disproportionately on men, dropped sharply. Women outlive men on average in every country. Our World in Data’s review (2023) attributes the gap partly to biology, since boys are more vulnerable from birth to prematurity, infections and some genetic disorders, and partly to behavior: accidents, violence, suicide and poisonings at young ages, and differences in smoking, drinking, drug use and occupational risk later in life. How large the behavioral share is, and how much of it reflects norms that could change, is where the debate lies.
stats.source_label: National Center for Health Statistics, Data Brief No. 548, “Mortality in the United States, 2024”

stats.label: Men’s share of US state and federal prisoners
stats.note: Men made up 93 percent of the 1.25 million people in US state and federal prisons at the end of 2023.
stats.detail: That was about 1,163,100 men and 91,100 women. The imprisonment rate for sentenced prisoners was 676 per 100,000 male residents against 51 per 100,000 female residents. Men also commit most violent crime and are most of its victims. Whether the gap reflects only differences in offending is disputed. A prison record sharply reduces later employment and marriage prospects, so incarceration feeds the gaps in work and family.
stats.source_label: Bureau of Justice Statistics, “Prisoners in 2023 – Statistical Tables”

stats.label: Young adults with a tertiary degree, OECD average
stats.note: Across OECD countries, 55 percent of women aged 25 to 34 held a tertiary degree in 2024, against 42 percent of men, a gap that widened slightly from 2019.
stats.detail: Tertiary covers short-cycle, bachelor’s, master’s and doctoral degrees; the bachelor’s alone is held by 29 percent of young women and 22 percent of young men. Young men are also more likely to lack an upper secondary qualification, 14 percent against 11 percent, and to stop at upper secondary or vocational post-secondary level, 44 percent against 34 percent. The previous edition, Education at a Glance 2024, found younger women ahead of younger men in every OECD country except Mexico. Those who see a structural problem for boys say a gap that appears across very different school systems and cultures points to a common cause, such as later male maturation or the changing labor market; others note that its size varies widely between countries, which suggests policy and culture matter.
stats.source_label: OECD, Education at a Glance 2025, “To what level have adults studied?”

stats.label: US boys ever diagnosed with ADHD
stats.note: About one boy in seven aged 5 to 17, 14.5 percent, had ever been diagnosed with ADHD in 2020–2022, against 8.0 percent of girls.
stats.detail: Across all children aged 5 to 17 the rate was 11.3 percent, and boys are also overrepresented among students in special education. The figures are read in opposite ways: as evidence that boys’ slower development of attention and self-regulation leaves many unready for the demands of early schooling, or as evidence that schools and clinicians pathologize ordinary boyish restlessness. Girls’ ADHD is thought to be underdiagnosed because it more often takes the inattentive form, which draws less notice in class.
stats.source_label: NCHS Data Brief No. 499, “Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder in Children Ages 5–17 Years”

stats.label: Employment of prime-age Americans without a four-year degree
stats.note: The share of men aged 25 to 54 without a four-year degree who had a job fell from 90 percent in 1979 to 81 percent in 2023, while the share for such women rose from 55 to 68 percent.
stats.detail: The report calls these adults working class; they are 64 percent of prime-age men and 57 percent of prime-age women. College-educated men’s employment dipped only slightly, from 96 to 93 percent, while college-educated women’s rose from 71 to 84 percent. Among working-class men the rate fell most for white men, from 91 to 82 percent, and Black working-class men had the lowest, falling from 79 to 74 percent. The institute puts working-class men’s median weekly earnings at $852 in 2023, only a fraction higher than in 1979 after inflation, while working-class women’s rose from $503 to $667. The source is a think tank that argues for male-focused policy, though its figures are tabulations of federal Current Population Survey data. Other analyses of wages differ by measure and years, and Heritage Foundation researchers argue that young men’s median earnings are similar, after inflation, to those of earlier generations, so the wage trend is less settled than the employment trend.
stats.source_label: American Institute for Boys and Men, “The State of Working Class Men” (corrected December 2024)

stats.label: Men’s share of US public school teachers
stats.note: Men were 23 percent of US public school teachers in 2020–21: 11 percent at the elementary level and 36 percent at the secondary level.
stats.detail: NCES found the share of men was not measurably different from 2011–12. Teaching is one of the HEAL occupations, in health, education, administration and literacy, where men are underrepresented: the American Institute for Boys and Men estimates that men hold 22 percent of HEAL jobs, about the same as women’s share of STEM jobs, and 12 percent of nursing jobs. Recruiting men into teaching and other HEAL work, on the model of decades of effort to bring women into science and engineering, is among the most common proposals in the debate; Governor Newsom’s 2025 executive order directed California’s education agencies to find ways to recruit more men as teachers.
stats.source_label: National Center for Education Statistics, Condition of Education, “Characteristics of Public School Teachers”

stats.label: US drug overdose death rate, by sex
stats.note: Men died of drug overdoses at more than twice women’s rate in 2024, 32.2 against 14.1 per 100,000, after both rates fell sharply from 2023.
stats.detail: There were 79,384 overdose deaths in the United States in 2024. The age-adjusted rate fell 27.3 percent for men and 23.0 percent for women from 2023, the largest one-year decrease in the period the brief covers. Overdoses, suicides and alcohol-related deaths, which the economists Anne Case and Angus Deaton call deaths of despair, have hit men without college degrees hardest, which is one reason the debate over male disadvantage is also a debate about class.
stats.source_label: National Center for Health Statistics, Data Brief No. 549, “Drug Overdose Deaths in the United States, 2023–2024”

stats.label: Americans who say women’s gains have not cost men
stats.note: In April 2024, 81 percent of US adults said women’s gains in society have not come at men’s expense, though 31 percent of Republican men said they have.
stats.detail: In a later Pew survey, fielded September 3 to 15, 2024, 39 percent of men but 21 percent of women said men are doing worse than 20 years ago at getting well-paying jobs, and 27 percent of men against 15 percent of women said men are doing worse at getting into college; 76 percent of all adults said women are doing better at getting leadership positions at work, against 27 percent who said the same of men. Republican men were the most likely to say men are losing ground, 43 percent on well-paying jobs against 18 percent of Democratic women. The views divide less by sex than by party, and by sex within party.
stats.source_label: Pew Research Center, “How Americans See Men and Masculinity”

stats.label: Gender gaps in 15-year-olds’ PISA scores, OECD average
stats.note: In PISA 2022, girls outscored boys by 24 points in reading on the OECD average and boys outscored girls by 9 points in mathematics, with no significant gap in science.
stats.detail: The reading gap is the larger and the more universal of the two: girls lead in almost every participating country, and by 40 points or more in Finland, Norway and Slovenia, while boys led in mathematics in 26 OECD countries. Reading and writing skills affect grades in every subject, which is one reason boys trail girls further in school marks than in mathematics tests.
stats.source_label: OECD, Society at a Glance 2024, “Student performance” (from PISA 2022)

stats.label: Men’s share of US workplace deaths
stats.note: Of 5,070 Americans killed on the job in 2024, 413 were women, so men accounted for about 92 percent.
stats.detail: Total workplace deaths fell 4.0 percent from 5,283 in 2023. Men dominate the most dangerous occupations, such as logging, roofing, fishing, construction and truck driving. The figure is cited by those who argue that the costs of traditional male roles are overlooked when gender gaps are discussed; others note that these jobs are also among the better-paid options open to men without degrees, and that their decline is part of what has left those men behind.
stats.source_label: US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Census of Fatal Occupational Injuries 2024

stats.label: Young adults lonely a lot of the previous day
stats.note: One in four young American men said they felt lonely a lot of the previous day, more than young American women (18 percent) and the median for young men across OECD countries (15 percent).
stats.detail: Gallup pooled its 2023 and 2024 World Poll data for the 38 OECD countries. Young US men stand out less for being lonely in absolute terms, since young men in Türkiye, France and Ireland report similar or higher rates, than for the size of their gap with other Americans; in some countries, such as Greece and Slovakia, young men are less lonely than other adults. Gallup has asked the question worldwide only since 2023, so it cannot show whether young men’s loneliness has risen. A single question about the previous day produces lower rates than the multi-item loneliness scales used in other surveys.
stats.source_label: Gallup, “Younger Men in the U.S. Among the Loneliest in West” (Gallup World Poll)

stats.label: Men who say women’s equality now discriminates against men
stats.note: Across 29 countries in 2026, 52 percent of men and 36 percent of women agreed that “we have gone so far in promoting women’s equality that we are discriminating against men.”
stats.detail: The survey, of 23,268 adults, measures perception, not discrimination itself. In the same survey 31 percent of Generation Z men agreed that a wife should always obey her husband, against 18 percent of Generation Z women (Ipsos, 2026), a gap between young men and young women that the survey’s authors highlight. Those who favor attention to boys and men read the figures as a warning that young men feel unseen and that the manosphere fills the gap; those who see a backlash read them as a sign that narratives of a boy crisis are turning men against gender equality.
stats.source_label: Ipsos and King’s College London, “Mind the Gaps: Global Attitudes Toward Gender Equality in 2026”

stats.label: US men who say they have no close friends
stats.note: The share of American men who say they have no close friends rose from 3 percent in 1990 to 15 percent in 2021, though the two figures come from different polls, so the change is approximate.
stats.detail: Over the same period the share of men with six or more close friends fell by half, from 55 to 27 percent. The Survey Center’s 2021 figures come from a survey of 2,019 adults fielded May 14 to 23, 2021, during the pandemic, and the 1990 figure is from a Gallup poll. Across all adults, 12 percent reported no close friends in 2021. Governor Newsom’s July 2025 executive order cited a related figure, that nearly one in four men under 30 report having no close friends, and the American Institute for Boys and Men reports that 21 percent of working-class men say they have none.
stats.source_label: Survey Center on American Life, Daniel A. Cox, “American Men Suffer a Friendship Recession”

questions.text: Should policy aim help at boys and men specifically, or at everyone who is struggling?
questions.why: The male gaps are real on average but much wider among poor, Black and working-class boys and men, and most proposed remedies could be offered to everyone. The dispute is whether sex is the right lens for policy.
questions.detail:
The case for male-specific help is that programs designed for everyone have not closed gaps that widened for decades. Boys and men are less likely to seek help, use counseling or enroll in college support programs, so a universal offer reaches them less. Supporters add that a gap running the other way would never be met with calls for sex-neutral policy. Targeted efforts, such as men’s health checks or mentoring for young men, can be designed and evaluated like any other policy, and supporters cite programs, such as certain career academies and mentoring models, that help boys much more than girls.

The case for universal programs is that need, not sex, is the better guide. Policy on poverty, school quality, good jobs and mental health care would reach the boys who struggle without implying that sex is the problem, and without competing with programs for girls. A universal offer can still be designed to reach boys, through where and how it is delivered, and targeting by sex can also be legally fraught under anti-discrimination law.

questions.text: Do schools shortchange boys, or do boys fall behind for reasons outside school?
questions.why: Boys get lower grades, more suspensions and more ADHD diagnoses, and read less well than girls almost everywhere. Observational data struggle to separate how schools teach and judge from how boys develop and the homes they grow up in.
questions.detail:
Those who say schools fit boys poorly start from development: boys gain self-control and verbal skills later than girls, yet schools ask for both from age five, reward organization and compliance in grades, and lean on reading and writing in every subject. Studies have found that teachers grade boys below what their test scores alone would predict, largely because of classroom behavior, and few elementary teachers are men; some studies find students do better with a teacher of their own sex. A Danish study by Thomas Dee and Hans Henrik Sievertsen found that starting school a year later sharply reduced inattention and hyperactivity, which suggests the timing of school matters, not only boys themselves.

Those who look outside school note that girls have outscored boys in US national reading tests since the 1970s, long before any recent change in schooling. Research by David Autor, David Figlio and colleagues on Florida siblings found that boys are more harmed than their sisters by family disadvantage. On this reading what has changed is the economy and family life around school, and gender gaps within the same income and racial group are small beside the gaps across them.

questions.text: Why have men pulled back from work: fewer good jobs, or changed incentives and choices?
questions.why: The fall in prime-age men’s labor force participation is concentrated among men without degrees. Economists agree on the trend and disagree on the mix of causes, which decides whether the remedy is economic policy or something else.
questions.detail:
The lost-jobs case ties the decline to the disappearance of well-paid manufacturing and other blue-collar work. David Autor, David Dorn and Gordon Hanson found that places hit hardest by Chinese import competition saw men’s employment and earnings fall, and marriage rates with them, as fewer men were seen as reliable partners. Wages for men without degrees have stagnated, so the reward for taking available work has fallen, and the unions that once raised their pay have shrunk. Rebuilding good non-college jobs through industrial policy, apprenticeships, wage subsidies or labor law would, on this view, bring many men back.

The incentives case notes that men have not returned to work in many places where jobs are available. The economists Ariel Binder and John Bound argue that falling demand for less-educated men’s labor “does not reasonably explain the data” on its own, and Mark Aguiar, Erik Hurst and colleagues estimated that better video games and recreational computing explain about half of the rise in leisure among young men since 2004. Disability benefits, opioid addiction, criminal records and the decline of marriage, which removes a reason to work, are also cited. On this view, jobs alone will not fix a problem that is partly about purpose and family.

questions.text: Is traditional masculinity part of the problem or part of the remedy?
questions.why: Everyone in the debate agrees that ideas about manhood shape men’s behavior. They disagree about whether the traditional script of strength, stoicism, self-reliance and providing is what hurts men or what they have lost.
questions.detail:
One side holds that the traditional script does the harm. Men who hold rigid ideas about manhood seek medical and psychological help less often, drink, take risks and use violence more, and are more isolated, and surveys link conformity to those norms with suicidal thoughts. The quarrel is with a script, not with men, boys or their instincts: it keeps courage, responsibility and protectiveness and rejects the emotional suppression and dominance packaged with them, and many on this side avoid the phrase toxic masculinity. A wider idea of manhood, open to caregiving and friendship, would let men take up growing jobs in health and education and share family life equally.

The other side holds that boys need a positive picture of what a good man is, and that telling them their instincts are toxic leaves them to find one in the online manosphere. Courage, responsibility, protectiveness and the drive to provide are virtues that families and communities depend on, and many men find purpose in being needed; the decline of marriage and of respected male roles has left them without it. Even some who favor male-specific policy, such as Richard Reeves, reject the language of toxic masculinity and call for a positive vision of masculinity rather than its removal.

questions.text: Does attention to boys and men threaten progress for women and girls?
questions.why: Money, attention and political energy are limited, and the debate over men is entangled with partisan politics and with online movements hostile to feminism. Whether naming men’s problems builds a coalition for fairness or feeds resentment is disputed.
questions.detail:
Those who say both can advance argue that proposals for boys, such as better early education, mental health care and vocational paths, add to what schools and health systems offer rather than divert it from girls, and that neglect breeds the very resentment critics fear. Taking those problems seriously within a framework that also supports women’s progress, as Richard Reeves, Governor Newsom and England’s men’s health strategy all say they do, is on this view the best defense against resentment.

Those who see a risk answer that the inequalities facing women, in pay, power, unpaid care and sexual violence, have not closed. A narrative of male crisis can recast women’s progress as the cause of men’s troubles and lend weight to the belief that equality has gone too far. Money and goodwill spent on a male agenda, they add, are likely to come out of programs for women and girls.

questions.text: Who is worse off on mental health: men, who die more, or girls and women, who report more distress?
questions.why: Men die by suicide and overdose far more often, while teenage girls report far more sadness and suicidal thoughts. Each side points to a measure that favors its reading.
questions.detail:
Those who see the deeper crisis among men say death is the hardest outcome to argue with: suicide, overdose, alcohol deaths and homicide all fall mostly on men. Men are less likely to recognize or report depression, so surveys of feelings understate their distress, and services built around talking about emotions reach them less. Governments from California to England have made men’s health and suicide prevention a priority for that reason.

Those who see greater distress among girls and women point out that they fare worse on almost every measure of reported mental health, from depression and anxiety to self-harm and suicide attempts, and that their reported distress rose through the 2010s. Suicide deaths reflect the lethality of the means used, above all firearms, as much as the depth of distress, so the male excess is partly a story about guns. Framing mental health as a male crisis, on this view, risks neglecting the larger number of girls and women who suffer and survive.

questions.text: Do schools, courts and governments treat males unfairly?
questions.why: Males receive most school suspensions and prison sentences. Whether that reflects bias or real differences in behavior and need is hard to test, and the answer differs by institution.
questions.detail:
Those who see bias argue that the gaps survive once conduct is accounted for. The law professor Sonja Starr’s 2015 study found federal sentences for men about 63 percent longer than for women after accounting for arrest offense, criminal history and other factors. Family courts long favored mothers in custody disputes, schools punish ordinary boyish behavior, and public bodies fund commissions and programs for women and girls but rarely for boys and men. If the same gaps ran against girls, they add, few would accept girls’ own behavior as the explanation.

Those who see the gaps as following behavior and choice answer that boys misbehave in class more and men commit most violent crime, so higher rates of discipline and imprisonment largely track conduct. Custody outcomes mostly reflect agreements between parents, and many states have moved toward equal parenting time. Men still hold most positions of power in politics, business and the courts said to discriminate against them, and programs for women were created to correct a long exclusion that has not fully ended.

positions.name: Close boys’ and men’s gaps with targeted policy
positions.steelman: Boys and men face real, specific gaps in school, work and health, and specific problems need specific remedies; closing them takes nothing from girls and women.
positions.detail:
These gaps are not caused by feminism, and closing them does not mean rolling back women’s gains, which are among the great achievements of the past century. The causes are mostly structural: schools that ask young boys for self-control and verbal skills they develop later than girls, an economy that has stripped away the well-paid jobs men without degrees relied on, and a culture that no longer offers men a clear, positive role as fathers and contributors. So recruit more men as teachers and counselors; give boys more time, including a later school start, and better vocational paths; bring men into the growing fields of health, education, administration and literacy as decades of effort brought women into science and engineering; design men’s health services that men will actually use; and treat fathers as full parents in law and policy.

We span the parties. Richard Reeves’s American Institute for Boys and Men stresses education and work; Governor Gavin Newsom’s order centers on suicide prevention, mentoring and service; England’s strategy is a health program; Virginia’s commission is bipartisan. To those who say the real problem is class or race: both matter, but the male gap shows up in most racial and income groups and widens with disadvantage, so class policy alone will not close it. To those who fear a contest with women: most of our proposals cost girls nothing, and leaving young men’s problems unaddressed hands them to people who do blame women.
positions.proponents: American Institute for Boys and Men; Richard Reeves; Gavin Newsom; UK Department of Health and Social Care; Virginia Commission on Boys and Men

positions.name: Restore marriage, fatherhood and confident manhood
positions.steelman: Men are adrift because marriage, fatherhood, faith and respect for manly virtue have decayed; rebuild the family and call men to responsibility.
positions.detail:
Boys raised without fathers are more likely to fail in school, drift out of work and get in trouble, and the collapse of marriage among working-class Americans has removed one of the strongest reasons men had to work and settle down. A culture that calls traditional masculinity toxic, and a benefits system that pays people not to work and penalizes marriage, have taught a generation of young men that they are not needed; screens, gaming and pornography fill the gap. As Senator Josh Hawley puts it, “the deconstruction of America begins with and depends on the deconstruction of American men.” The remedy is to rebuild the family: end marriage penalties in tax and welfare programs, require work, support fathers in custody and child support law, protect children from addictive technology, and call men to responsibility rather than telling them to become more like women.

We do not want to roll back women’s gains; we want strong families in which mothers and fathers both matter, and marriage benefits women and children as well as men. Men’s earnings have not fallen enough to explain the collapse of marriage and work, and jobs go unfilled while men stay idle. The virtues others call toxic are what make men good fathers, workers and citizens. Government cannot replace a father, and new programs will fail if the family keeps eroding.
positions.proponents: Heritage Foundation; Josh Hawley; Aaron M. Renn

positions.name: Free men from restrictive masculine norms
positions.steelman: Men are hurt by a narrow script of control, stoicism and self-reliance; widen what manhood can mean and men will live healthier, less isolated lives.
positions.detail:
That script keeps men from doctors and therapists, from close friendships, from caring work and from their children’s lives, and it makes some of them angry and violent when they cannot live up to it. Economic anxiety turns it into a crisis: when men cannot earn what the script demands, they feel they have failed as men. Equimundo’s 2025 survey found that men who adhere to restrictive masculine norms are 6.27 times more likely to report suicidal thoughts, and men facing economic insecurity 16.3 times more likely. The American Psychological Association’s 2018 guidelines for work with boys and men conclude that conformity to traditional masculinity ideology limits males’ psychological development and harms their mental and physical health.

The answer is neither to abandon men nor to restore the old script but to widen it: raise boys to value emotional honesty, friendship and care; build mental health services tailored to men; engage fathers as caregivers; mentor young men; challenge the online influencers who sell them grievance; and pair all of this with economic security for every man. We criticize a set of expectations, not men. Courage, responsibility and protectiveness are welcome; it is the emotional suppression and dominance bundled with them that show up in suicide, isolation and violence. Gender equality is good for men too.
positions.proponents: Equimundo; American Psychological Association; Niobe Way

positions.name: Tackle class and race inequality for everyone
positions.steelman: There is no general crisis of boys and men, but poor, Black, Hispanic and working-class boys who are struggling badly; help every young person who struggles, boys included.
positions.detail:
Affluent boys are doing very well, and the differences between rich and poor, or between racial groups, are far larger than those between boys and girls within them. Men as a group still earn more and hold most positions of power, while girls report far more depression and face far more sexual violence. Raj Chetty and colleagues found that the usual gender gap in employment reverses for children raised in poor families, whose sons are less likely to work as adults than their daughters, while among affluent families men still work more than women. As Steven Roberts of Monash University writes, boys’ educational challenges “intersect with poverty, racism, and structural inequality more than gender alone,” and talk of a crisis of masculinity has recurred for 150 years, each time isolating gender from the forces that drive outcomes.

Framing the problem as men against women invites the conclusion that women’s progress is to blame, a conclusion the manosphere is eager to draw, and the sociologist Jessica Calarco argues that a male-focused agenda weakens support for the universal programs that would help struggling men. So reduce child poverty, improve schools in poor neighborhoods, expand mental health care, raise wages and rebuild unions. Male suicide and early death are real and deserve attention through health policy, gun safety and addiction treatment, none of which needs a story of gender crisis. And the decline of marriage follows the decline of working-class economic security, not the other way round.
positions.proponents: Steven Roberts; Jessica Calarco; American Association of University Women

positions.name: End discrimination against boys and men
positions.steelman: Boys and men are not only falling behind; schools, courts and governments treat them unfairly, and equal treatment means naming that discrimination too.
positions.detail:
The language of discrimination has been reserved for women, so the unfairness males face is rarely named. Schools discipline boys more harshly for ordinary boyish behavior; as the American Enterprise Institute describes Christina Hoff Sommers’s book The War Against Boys, “Under the guise of helping girls, many schools have adopted policies that penalize boys, often for simply being masculine.” The law professor Sonja Starr’s 2015 study of federal cases found that men received sentences about 63 percent longer than women after controlling for the arrest offense and criminal history. Health systems fund women’s health offices but neglect men’s; and governments run many commissions for women and girls but almost none for boys and men.

Equal treatment means the same scrutiny for disadvantages that fall on males: commissions on the status of boys and men with the same standing as those for women, shared parenting as the default after divorce, equal attention to men’s health, and school practices that do not punish boys for being boys. No school would explain away a disparity running against girls by saying that girls misbehave. The men at the top are not the boys at the bottom, and a powerful few do not make the many privileged. Some of us, like Sommers, are equity feminists who support women’s legal equality; others, like the National Coalition for Men, work through litigation and advocacy on custody, sentencing and sex-based programs.
positions.proponents: National Coalition for Men; Christina Hoff Sommers

crux.lead: Do boys and men fall behind because they are male, or because they are disadvantaged?
crux.lead_highlight: because they are male, or because they are disadvantaged
crux.subtitle: Most other arguments here turn on this one. If something about being male in today’s schools, jobs and culture drives the gaps, they call for answers aimed at males. If poverty, race and lost working-class jobs drive them, landing harder on boys, the answer is to fight disadvantage itself.
crux.empirical: The testable part is how much of each gap remains between boys and girls raised in the same families, neighborhoods and incomes. Sibling and equal-income studies cut both ways: the male gap is largest among the poor, which fits the class reading, but it arises because boys fare worse than their sisters under the same conditions, which fits the sex-specific one. Trials of boys’ programs against equal spending on everyone would add more.
crux.values: No data settles whether sex should guide public attention and spending while women still earn less and hold less power, or whether help should follow need alone, nor what a good man is. Some see the fading of husband, father and provider as a loss in itself, others as progress men have yet to catch up with, and others want each person treated alike, whatever the averages show.

actions.title: Explore federal data on boys and girls in school
actions.description: The National Center for Education Statistics’ Condition of Education gathers the official US indicators on enrollment, achievement, dropout, college going and teachers, most of them broken down by sex.

actions.title: Follow the American Institute for Boys and Men
actions.description: Richard Reeves’s think tank publishes research and policy proposals on boys’ education, men’s work and health, and fatherhood.
actions.for_position: Close boys’ and men’s gaps with targeted policy

actions.title: Support fathers through the National Fatherhood Initiative
actions.description: A nonprofit that supplies fatherhood program curricula and training to community groups, agencies and correctional facilities, and promotes fathers’ involvement in their children’s lives.
actions.for_position: Restore marriage, fatherhood and confident manhood

actions.title: Read Equimundo’s State of American Men 2025
actions.description: A survey-based report on men’s economic anxiety, isolation and mental health, and on how rigid ideas about manhood relate to suicidal thoughts and political attitudes, with recommendations for policy.
actions.for_position: Free men from restrictive masculine norms

actions.title: Support the American Association of University Women
actions.description: A long-standing organization that researches and advocates for equity for women and girls in education and work, and whose research has argued that race and income gaps in schooling outweigh gaps by sex.
actions.for_position: Tackle class and race inequality for everyone

actions.title: Know the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline
actions.description: Calling or texting 988 in the United States reaches trained crisis counselors at any hour, for anyone in distress or worried about someone else.

actions.title: Read Pew’s report on how Americans see men and masculinity
actions.description: A 2024 national survey on how Americans think men are doing at work, in college and in relationships, which traits they value in men, and how views split by sex and party.

actions.title: Mentor a young person with Big Brothers Big Sisters
actions.description: The national mentoring network matches adult volunteers with children and teenagers in their own community for one-to-one mentoring.

actions.title: Support a state commission on boys and men
actions.description: Virginia created a permanent state commission on boys and men in 2026; its backers’ site describes the commission’s work and the model for similar bills, including Washington’s, which failed for a fifth time in 2026.
actions.for_position: Close boys’ and men’s gaps with targeted policy

actions.title: Read the National Coalition for Men’s case
actions.description: A men’s rights organization founded in 1977 that campaigns and litigates on custody, sentencing, sex-based programs and what it describes as discrimination against boys and men.
